13730: A reservoir is a place where a large amount of something — most often a liquid — is collected, held, and stored so that it can be used when needed. Think of it as a "savings account," but instead of money, it stores things like water, oil, or even ideas. The defining quality of a reservoir is that it acts as a supply that you draw from over time — it is not just a passing flow, but a stored body that stays put.

When most people say "reservoir," they mean a large body of stored water, usually meant to supply a city, town, or farming region.

Reservoirs of this kind come in two forms:

1. Man-made (artificial) reservoirs — These are the most common type. Humans build a dam across a river, which blocks the natural flow of water. As the water has nowhere to go, it backs up and collects, forming a huge lake behind the dam. That lake is the reservoir. Cities then pipe water from it for people to drink, cook with, and bathe in. A good example is the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, which created Lake Mead — one of the largest reservoirs in the world.

2. Natural reservoirs — Sometimes, a natural lake or even a large underground layer of rock acts as a reservoir. The water simply gathered there over thousands of years on its own, and humans tap into it.

The key point is the purpose: a reservoir is not just any lake. It is water that is being managed and stored for a specific use.

A reservoir does not have to sit on the surface. Deep underground, porous rock (rock full of tiny holes, like a sponge) can be soaked with water, oil, or natural gas. These underground pockets of stored liquid or gas are also called reservoirs. When an oil company drills a well, they are drilling down to reach an oil reservoir — a layer of rock that has been holding oil for millions of years.

In the same way, underground water reservoirs (called aquifers) supply wells across the world. Many farms and rural homes depend entirely on water pumped up from these hidden reservoirs.

The word is also used for small containers inside machines or devices that store a liquid needed for the machine to work.

For example:

  • A car has a brake fluid reservoir — a small plastic tank under the hood that stores the fluid needed to make the brakes work.
  • A fountain pen has an ink reservoir — the chamber inside the pen that holds the ink.
  • A car's windshield wiper system has a washer fluid reservoir.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: a dedicated holding space that stores a liquid so it is ready to be used as needed.

Because a reservoir suggests a large, deep, available supply, people also use the word figuratively — meaning they apply it to things that are not physical liquids at all.

You might hear or read sentences like:

  • "She has a deep reservoir of patience." — She has a great deal of patience stored within her, ready to be drawn on.
  • "The country has a vast reservoir of talent." — There are many talented people available in that country.
  • "His years of experience gave him a reservoir of knowledge." — He has accumulated so much knowledge that he can draw from it like water from a well.

In all these cases, the speaker is painting a picture: just as a water reservoir is a large, dependable store you can draw from, this person or place has a large, dependable store of something valuable.

In science, especially in medicine and biology, reservoir has a very specific meaning. It refers to a species, animal, or environment that permanently carries and harbors a disease-causing germ (like a virus or bacteria) without being seriously harmed by it itself.

For example, bats are considered a natural reservoir for certain viruses. The virus lives inside the bat population across generations. The bats generally do not get sick from it, but the virus can sometimes jump from bats to humans, causing outbreaks. In this sense, the bat population is the "storage place" for the virus — it is where the germ lives and waits, just like water waits in a dam.
What Ties All These Meanings Together

No matter which context you see the word "reservoir" in, three ideas are always present:

  1. Storage — Something is being held and kept, not just passing through.
  2. Quantity — There is a significant amount of whatever is being stored.
  3. Future use — The stored thing is being kept precisely because it will be needed and drawn from later.

If you remember these three ideas — stored, substantial, and available for use — you will understand the word "reservoir" correctly in any sentence you ever encounter it.
13731:
To reside somewhere means to live there as your home — in a settled, established way. It is not about visiting a place or passing through. It means that place is where you actually belong, sleep, and have made your life.

"She resides in Tokyo."

This means Tokyo is her home. She lives there. It is where her life is based.

"Reside" and "live" mean almost the same thing, but there is an important difference in tone and formality.

  • "Live" is the everyday, casual word. You use it in normal conversation.
  • "Reside" is the formal version. You see it in official documents, legal papers, news articles, and formal writing.

Think of it this way: you would say "Where do you live?" to a friend at a coffee shop. But a government form would ask "State the city where you currently reside."

Both sentences ask for the same information. The word "reside" just sounds more serious, official, and polished.

This is a critical distinction. "Reside" always implies permanence or long-term settlement. It is not temporary.

  • If you are at a hotel for three days → you are staying there, not residing.
  • If you are visiting your parents for a week → you are visiting, not residing.
  • If you moved to a city and that is now your home → you reside there.

The idea of roots, stability, and an established home is baked into the meaning of "reside." A person who resides somewhere has made it their base of life — not just a temporary stop.

Here is where "reside" becomes even more interesting. The word is also used beyond physical places. It can describe where a quality, a power, a feeling, or an idea "lives" — meaning where it exists or is found.

"True power resides in the people, not in the government."

This does not mean people literally live inside something. It means power belongs to, is located in, or is held by the people. The power has its "home" there.

More examples of this figurative use:

"The real problem resides in the way the system was designed."

→ The problem is found within the design itself.

"Wisdom does not reside in age alone."

→ Wisdom is not simply located in or guaranteed by old age.

"The final decision resides with the manager."

→ The authority to decide belongs to, and sits with, the manager.

In all these cases, think of "reside" as asking: "Where does this thing have its home? Where does it belong or exist?" — and then answering that question.

Reside is always followed by a preposition. The most common ones are:

  • reside in → used with cities, countries, buildings, or abstract things
    "He resides in Canada." / "The issue resides in the code."*
  • reside at → used with a specific address
    "She resides at 14 Elm Street."*
  • reside with → used when authority, power, or a right belongs to someone
    "The final say resides with the committee."*

Since you want to fully understand this word, knowing its family will help you recognize it in different forms:

  • Resident (noun) → a person who resides somewhere
    "She is a resident of New York."*
  • Residence (noun) → the place where someone resides; the act of residing
    "His residence is in the countryside." / "She took up residence in Rome."*
  • Residential (adjective) → relating to where people reside
    "This is a quiet, residential neighborhood."*
  • Residing (present participle) → the ongoing action
    "The family residing in that house has lived there for decades."*

DimensionDetail
Basic meaningTo live somewhere as your established home
ToneFormal — used in official, legal, and serious writing
Key ideaPermanence and settlement — not temporary
Figurative useWhere something (power, quality, problem) exists or belongs
Common prepositionsin, at, with

The single most important thing to remember: "reside" is the formal way of saying "live in a place as your home," and it can also describe where something non-physical — like power, truth, or a problem — is found or belongs.
13732: Residence means the place where a person lives, or the fact/state of living in a particular place. It is a formal, slightly official-sounding word. When you think of "residence," think of it as the more serious, grown-up version of words like "home" or "house."
The Two Main Layers of Meaning

This one word carries two related but distinct ideas. Understanding both is key.

1. A Place Where Someone Lives

This is the most common use. Here, "residence" refers to the physical building or location a person calls home — particularly on a long-term or permanent basis.

"The doctor's residence was a quiet apartment near the hospital."
"Please write your current residence on the form."
"The ambassador's residence was a grand old building in the city."

Notice that it doesn't just mean any building — it means the place where someone actually lives. A hotel room you stay in for two nights is not your residence. The flat where you sleep every night, keep your belongings, and return to after work — that is your residence.

2. The Act or State of Living Somewhere

Here, "residence" refers not to the building itself, but to the fact that someone lives (or lived) in a particular place, and often for how long.

"After ten years of residence in Canada, he applied for citizenship."
"Her residence in that village lasted only two summers."
"The law requires five years of continuous residence before you qualify."

In this sense, you are not talking about a building — you are talking about the condition, the period, the status of being a resident of a place.

"Residence" is frequently used in formal, legal, and official settings. This is because it carries a sense of permanence and legitimacy that casual words like "home" do not.

On government forms and legal documents:
"Place of residence" is the official phrase used to ask where you permanently live.

"State your place of residence: _"

For important or official homes:
Leaders, dignitaries, and heads of state often have an official residence — a home that comes with their position, not just a private house they own.

"10 Downing Street is the official residence of the British Prime Minister."
"Rashtrapati Bhavan is the official residence of the President of India."

When someone is described as being "in residence" at a place (especially a university, institution, or organization), it means they are officially stationed there for a period of time — living and working there as part of a formal arrangement.

"She was appointed as the writer in residence at the university for one year."
"The sculptor is currently in residence at the arts centre."
"The doctor completed his training while in residence at the hospital."

This phrase signals an official, recognized presence — not just a casual visit.

Understanding a word fully also means knowing how it differs from words that seem similar.

Residence vs. House
A house is just the physical structure — the walls, roof, and rooms. A residence is a house (or flat, or any dwelling) considered as the place someone lives in. Every residence is a building of some kind, but not every building is a residence.

Residence vs. Home
Home is warm and emotional — it suggests belonging, comfort, family, memory. Residence is neutral and formal — it describes where you live as a fact, not a feeling. You would say "home" to your friends; you would write "residence" on a legal document.

Residence vs. Address
Your address is simply the string of information (street number, city, pin code) that locates you on a map. Your residence is the actual place where you live. Your address tells people where to find your residence. The two are closely linked, but they are not the same thing.

Residence vs. Accommodation
Accommodation just means a place provided for someone to stay — it could be temporary (a hotel, a hostel). Residence implies something more settled and permanent.

One of the most important things to understand about "residence" is that it carries a strong sense of permanence or at least long-term staying. It is not about short visits.

If you spend a weekend in another city, that hotel is not your residence. If you live in a city for years, working, paying bills, building a life — that city is your place of residence.

This is why "residence" matters so much in legal and official contexts: governments, banks, and institutions want to know where you truly, stably live — not where you are passing through.

Here are the most important phrases you will encounter with this word:

PhraseMeaning
  • Place of residence — where you officially live; used on forms
  • Primary/permanent residence — the main place where you live long-term, as opposed to a holiday home
  • Official residence — a home tied to an official position or role
  • Country of residence — the country you currently live in
  • Take up residence — to begin living in a new place
  • In residence — officially stationed at and living/working at a place
  • Legal residence — where you are officially registered as living, for legal purposes
  • Proof of residence — a document (like a utility bill or bank statement) that proves you live at an address

Residence, as a noun, means:

  1. The place where a person lives, especially permanently or long-term — a formal, official way to refer to someone's home.
  2. The state or period of living in a place — the fact that someone resides somewhere, and for how long.

It is a word associated with formality, officialdom, and permanence. You will encounter it on forms, in legal documents, in news about heads of state, and in descriptions of academic or artistic appointments. It is never a casual or emotional word — it is precise, neutral, and serious.
13733:
Residency means the condition or state of living in a particular place. When you are a resident somewhere — meaning you actually live there, not just visit — that act or status of living there is called your residency.

But this single word has grown to carry several distinct and important meanings depending on the context. Each meaning is connected to this core idea of "being stationed somewhere for a period of time," but they play out very differently in real life.
Meaning 1: The General Sense — Living Somewhere

In its most ordinary use, residency simply refers to the fact of living in a place, especially on a long-term or official basis.

"Her residency in Mumbai spans over twenty years."

Here, it just means the ongoing condition of making a place your home. It is not about visiting or passing through — it implies a settled, stable presence.
Meaning 2: Legal Residency — The Right to Live in a Country

This is one of the most commonly encountered uses, especially in legal, immigration, and governmental contexts.

Legal residency refers to the officially recognised status that allows a person to live in a country or region where they are not a citizen. Governments issue this status (often called a "residency permit" or "permanent residency") to foreigners who meet certain conditions — such as having a job, family ties, or fulfilling an investment requirement.

This is different from citizenship. A person with residency has the legal right to live and often work in a country, but they may not have the full rights of a citizen — such as voting. "Permanent residency" (sometimes called "PR") means this right has no expiry date, though it usually comes with conditions too. "Temporary residency" means the right is granted only for a fixed period.

"She applied for permanent residency in Canada after living there on a work visa for three years."

The key idea here: residency is a legal status granted by an authority that permits someone to be in a place as an official inhabitant.
Meaning 3: Medical Residency — The Training Period for Doctors

This is a specialised but extremely widespread use of the word, particularly in countries like the United States, India, and many others.

After a person earns their medical degree (becoming a doctor in the basic sense), they are not yet fully qualified to practise independently. They must spend a period — typically anywhere from three to seven or more years — working under supervision at a hospital, gaining hands-on clinical experience in their chosen specialisation. This period of supervised, immersive, practical training is called a residency.

The doctor in this phase is called a resident. They work long hours, treat real patients, make real decisions — but always under the oversight of senior doctors. The word "residency" here comes from the old tradition of doctors literally residing (living) at the hospital during their training, though today residents do not always live on-site.

"After finishing her MBBS, she matched into a residency programme in cardiology at a teaching hospital in Delhi."

The key idea here: a residency is a structured, official period of professional training embedded within an institution, where the trainee both learns and works at the same time.
Meaning 4: Artist or Academic Residency — A Creative or Scholarly Placement

In the world of arts, literature, music, and academia, a residency refers to a period during which a creative person or scholar is formally hosted by an institution — such as a university, arts centre, gallery, or cultural organisation — to pursue a project, create work, or engage with the community there.

The institution typically provides the person with a workspace, funding, housing, or some combination of these. In exchange, the artist or academic may give lectures, hold workshops, exhibit work, or simply create during their time there.

"The novelist was awarded a six-month residency at a writers' retreat in the mountains, where she completed her second book."

"The university offered him a residency as a poet-in-residence, where he would run workshops for students."

The key idea here: a residency is a temporary but immersive period of focused work, made possible by an institution that invests in you and your work.
Meaning 5: Performance Residency — Repeated Shows at One Venue

This use is very common in the music and entertainment world. When a musician, band, DJ, or performer is booked to perform multiple times at the same venue — rather than a single one-off show — that ongoing engagement is called a residency.

"The jazz band held a weekly residency at a popular club in Bangalore every Friday night."

"The pop star announced a six-week residency at the O2 Arena in London."

This meaning comes from the same root idea: instead of touring from city to city, the performer stays (resides) at one place for a sustained period. It has become a prestigious model in the music industry — artists like Adele and Celine Dion have done famous residencies in Las Vegas, for example.
Meaning 6: Official Residence — A Building or Place of Stay

Less commonly, "residency" can also refer to a physical building or compound that serves as an official or formal home — especially in a historical or diplomatic context.

"The Governor's residency was a large colonial building at the edge of the city."

In this sense, it is close to saying "the official residence" — the place where someone of authority or importance formally lives.

Notice how all these uses share the same underlying thread: being in one place, in an established and purposeful way, for a meaningful period of time.

Whether it is a migrant earning the legal right to stay in a country, a young doctor planted in a hospital to learn their craft, a novelist nestled in a mountain retreat to write, or a band taking up regular nights at a jazz club — in each case, someone is residing somewhere with intention and structure. That is what "residency" captures.

• General: The condition or state of living somewhere — "twenty years of residency in this city."
  • Legal/Immigration: An official status granting the right to live in a country — "permanent residency," "residency permit."
  • Medical: A post-degree training period for doctors inside a hospital — "surgical residency," "she is in her second year of residency."
  • Arts/Academia: A formal period of creative or scholarly work hosted by an institution — "artist residency," "writer-in-residence."
  • Performance/Music: A recurring engagement at a single venue — "the band has a residency at that club every weekend."
  • Physical place: The official home or building of an authority — "the governor's residency."
13734:
A resident is a person who lives in a particular place — not just passing through, not on a short visit, but actually based there in an ongoing, settled way.

The key idea locked inside this word is permanence (or at least, long-term presence). A resident has planted their life, however partially, in a specific location.

When people say someone is a resident of a place, they mean that place is where that person calls home — where they sleep, where they receive mail, where their daily life happens.

"She is a resident of Mumbai."
"The residents of this building complained about the noise."
"Long-time residents of the village remember when this road didn't exist."

Notice that "resident" can refer to someone living in a country, a city, a neighborhood, an apartment building, or even a specific institution like a care home or hostel. The word scales across all these levels.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where precision really matters. Several words seem similar but mean different things:

  • A visitor or tourist is in a place temporarily — a few days or weeks. They are not residents.
  • A guest is invited and temporary by nature.
  • A citizen is a legal member of a country (by birth or naturalization). A citizen has rights tied to belonging. A resident, on the other hand, simply lives there — without necessarily having those full legal rights of citizenship.
  • A tenant is someone who rents a property. They can also be a resident, but "tenant" emphasizes the rental relationship, while "resident" emphasizes the act of living there.

You can be a resident without being a citizen — this is very common. For example, someone from India living and working in Canada with a visa is a resident of Canada but not a Canadian citizen. They live there, but they haven't been granted full legal membership in that country.
The Legal Sense: "Legal Resident" or "Permanent Resident"

In formal, legal, or immigration contexts, "resident" takes on a more precise meaning.

A legal resident (or permanent resident) is someone who has been officially granted the right to live in a country by its government — even though they are not a citizen of that country. Many countries have a formal status for this.

"She applied to become a permanent resident of the United States."
"He holds permanent resident status in Australia."

This is distinct from someone who is living in a country without official permission, or on a temporary visa. Those people are physically residing there, but they may not hold the official status of "legal resident."

So in everyday speech, any person who lives in a place can be called a resident. But in legal speech, a "resident" (especially with words like "legal," "permanent," or "lawful" in front) refers to someone who has government-approved status to live there long-term.

This is a completely separate but very common meaning, especially in healthcare.

In medicine, a resident (also called a resident doctor or simply a resident) is a doctor who has graduated from medical school but is still in a period of supervised, hands-on training inside a hospital or clinic. They are qualified doctors — they've earned their degree — but they are not yet independent specialists. They are learning under the guidance of more experienced doctors.

"The resident examined the patient before the senior doctor arrived."
"She worked 80-hour weeks as a first-year resident."
"He's doing his residency in cardiology." (Here, "residency" is the noun form of the training period itself.)

The connection to the original meaning is historical — in the past, these trainee doctors literally lived (resided) in the hospital. That practice has faded, but the name stuck.

A resident doctor sits between a medical student (who is still studying) and a fully independent consultant or specialist (who has completed all training). They have real responsibility for patients but are still supervised and learning.

In places like care homes, nursing homes, rehabilitation centers, boarding schools, or hostels, the people who live there are called residents.

"The residents of the nursing home gathered in the common room."
"Each resident has their own room."

This usage simply emphasizes that these people live in the institution as their primary home, often long-term. It's a respectful, neutral term — preferred over words that might suggest they are merely patients or inmates.

Resident as a noun always points to one thing: a person who lives in a place with some degree of continuity and settlement. The exact shade of meaning shifts depending on context:

  • In everyday use: someone who lives in a city, town, building, or neighborhood.
  • In legal/immigration use: someone officially permitted to live in a country long-term without being a citizen.
  • In medicine: a qualified doctor in a structured training program at a hospital.
  • In institutional use: someone who lives in a care home, school, or similar facility.

What ties all these uses together is the same underlying idea — this person belongs to this place, at least for now, in a way that a passerby or visitor simply does not.
13735:
Residential means relating to, used for, or suitable for the purpose of living.

The root of the idea is a residence — which is simply a place where a person lives. So whenever you use the word "residential," you are pointing to something that is connected to the act of living somewhere, rather than working, shopping, or running a business.
The Most Common Use: Describing Places

The most frequent way "residential" is used is to describe a type of area, building, or space.

A residential area (or residential neighborhood) is a part of a town or city where people live — it is filled with houses, apartments, and flats. It is quiet, domestic, and meant for people to call home. It is not a place for factories, offices, or large shops. When you walk through a residential street, you see front doors, gardens, children playing, and parked cars belonging to families.

A residential building is a building designed so that people can live inside it — an apartment block, a block of flats, or a housing complex. It is not an office building (where people work) or a warehouse (where goods are stored).

"The city plans to convert the old factory into residential apartments."
Here, the factory — which was used for manufacturing — will be turned into homes for people to live in.

"He grew up in a quiet residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Mumbai."
The neighborhood is peaceful and domestic — full of homes, not businesses.
Contrasting with Other Types of Property/Zones

Understanding what "residential" is not makes it even clearer.

In city planning and real estate, land and buildings are divided into categories:

  • Residential → for living (homes, flats, apartments)
  • Commercial → for doing business (shops, offices, restaurants, hotels)
  • Industrial → for manufacturing or storage (factories, warehouses)

So if someone says, "This area is zoned for residential use only," it means that only homes can be built or run there — no shops, no factories, nothing commercial. This distinction matters enormously in legal, architectural, and planning contexts.

"Residential" is also used to describe a place where people both live and receive a service — usually care or support.

A residential care home (also called a residential facility or residential home) is a place where people — often elderly people, people with disabilities, or children without family support — live permanently or long-term and receive professional care, meals, and supervision from staff.

The key idea here is that residents are not just visiting during the day. They live there. This is what makes it "residential" care — the care is provided at the place where the person resides.

"After her surgery, she moved into a residential care facility where nurses could look after her around the clock."

This is different from, say, a day-care center or a clinic, where you go for a few hours and then return home.

Another important use: when a course, training program, or school is described as "residential," it means that the participants do not just attend classes and go home at the end of the day. Instead, they live at the venue for the duration of the program — sleeping there, eating there, and spending their time there.

A residential school (like a boarding school) is a school where students live on campus in dormitories during the school term.

A residential workshop or residential retreat is a multi-day program where attendees stay at the location — often in rooms provided by the organizers — rather than commuting from their own homes.

"She attended a five-day residential writing workshop in the hills of Himachal Pradesh."
She stayed at the workshop venue for five days — it was not a day event.

The common thread: to be there in a "residential" sense means to be living there, not just visiting.

In formal or legal language, "residential" is also used to describe information about where someone lives.

Your residential address is simply the address where you currently live — your home address. This is different from your work address or a postal address.

Residential status refers to the legal classification of where a person officially resides — particularly for purposes like taxation, immigration, or government registration. For example, your "residential status" in a country determines whether you are taxed as a local resident or as a foreign visitor. In banking or legal paperwork, you will often be asked to provide proof of your "residential address" — a document that confirms where you live (like a utility bill or a rental agreement).

"Please provide a document as proof of your residential address."
They want official proof of where you live.

Across every single use — whether it's a neighborhood, a care home, a school, a course, or a legal status — the word "residential" always connects back to one fundamental idea:

The act and condition of living somewhere.

If people sleep there, call it home, or are classified by where they live, the word "residential" applies. If a space is designed so people can reside in it, it is residential. If a program requires you to live on-site rather than commute, it is residential.

It is the adjective that marks something as belonging to the world of homes, dwelling, and living — as opposed to the worlds of commerce, work, or industry.

Whenever you see "residential," ask yourself: Is this connected to the idea of people living somewhere?

  • Residential street → Yes, people live there.
  • Residential care → Yes, people live there and receive care.
  • Residential course → Yes, participants live at the venue during the course.
  • Residential address → Yes, it's the address where you live.

If the answer is yes — if the thing is about living somewhere — "residential" is the right word.
13736:
Imagine you fill a glass with juice and drink most of it. You set it down and walk away. Later, you notice a thin film of juice still coating the inside of the glass — a little sticky, a little colored. You didn't drink it, it didn't evaporate entirely, and it wasn't washed away. It simply stayed behind.

That leftover film is what "residual" describes. Something residual is what persists, lingers, or remains after the main part has been removed, used up, finished, or dealt with.

Residual means: remaining after the main part of something has ended, been removed, or been resolved.

It describes whatever is left over — the trace, the remnant, the lingering portion — that survives a process which was largely completed but not perfectly or entirely so.
The Two Core Ideas Inside This Word

Whenever you use "residual," two things are always implied:

  1. Something larger existed before. There was a whole — a full dose of medicine, a complete emotion, a large quantity of a substance, a serious problem.
  2. Most of it is gone, but not all of it. A process happened — time passed, treatment occurred, something was cleaned or resolved — but it wasn't 100% thorough. A smaller, weaker, or diminished portion survived.

That surviving portion is residual.

"Residual" always carries the sense of lingering or persisting. The thing it describes tends to be:

  • Smaller or weaker than the original
  • Stubborn — it didn't go away when most things did
  • Often unwanted — though not always
  • A consequence or trace of something that came before

In everyday experience:

After a house fire is extinguished, the building is no longer burning. But weeks later, the walls may still carry a faint smoky smell. That smell is residual — the fire is gone, but its effect lingers in a diminished form.

After you cry, the main emotion may pass. But you might still feel a dull heaviness for hours afterward. That lingering emotional weight is residual sadness.

In medicine and health:

A patient recovers from a stroke. The acute medical crisis is over. But the patient still has slight weakness in one hand. Doctors call this residual weakness or residual deficit — the illness is largely resolved, but its effects haven't entirely disappeared.

Chemotherapy kills a tumor. Doctors later detect a small cluster of surviving cancer cells. Those cells are described as residual disease — most of the cancer is gone, but not all.

In science and the environment:

Farmers spray pesticides on crops. Rain and sunlight break them down over weeks. But some amount of the chemical persists in the soil, still active but much reduced. Scientists call this the residual effect of the pesticide — or describe the remaining chemical as residual pesticide.

After an oil spill is cleaned up, some oil seeps into rock and sediment where it cannot be easily reached. That is residual oil — what the cleanup couldn't remove.

In psychology and emotions:

Someone who was bullied as a child grows into a confident adult. The trauma no longer dominates their life. But they notice they become unusually tense in certain situations that remind them of the past. That tension is residual — it's the leftover psychological impact of an experience that is otherwise far in the past.

You have an argument with a friend, and you eventually make up. But for a few days you feel a slight awkwardness around them. That is residual discomfort — the dispute is resolved, but its emotional trace hasn't fully faded.

In engineering and physics:

When a magnetized metal bar is demagnetized, most of its magnetism is removed. But a small amount of magnetic force remains. This is called residual magnetism — it's what stubbornly stays even after the demagnetizing process ends.

After a machine is turned off and cools down, it may still vibrate very faintly for a few moments. That is residual vibration.

In statistics and data:

When analysts build a mathematical model to predict something (like house prices), the model rarely predicts perfectly. The gap between what the model predicts and what actually happened is called residual error or simply a residual — it's the unexplained leftover that the model couldn't account for.

In finance and business:

A car bought for ₹10 lakh loses value over time. After five years, it might be worth ₹3 lakh. That ₹3 lakh is called the residual value of the car — it's what remains of its original worth after depreciation.

In entertainment (a specific usage):

Actors in films and TV shows sometimes earn residual payments — payments they receive each time their work is re-aired, streamed, or rebroadcast. These are called "residuals" because they come after the original work is done, as a continuing financial remainder of that original effort.

You might wonder how "residual" differs from words like remaining, leftover, or lingering. Here's the key distinction:

  • Remaining simply means "not yet gone" — it doesn't necessarily imply that a process happened.
  • Leftover is informal and usually physical (leftover food).
  • Residual is more precise and formal. It specifically implies that (a) a larger whole existed, (b) a significant process worked on it and largely resolved it, and (c) what you're describing is the smaller, often persistent remainder of that process.

"Residual" is the right word when you want to emphasize that something is a trace or remnant of something larger that is mostly over.
How to Know When to Use "Residual"

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Was there something larger or more intense before?
  2. Did a process significantly reduce or eliminate it?
  3. Is there a smaller, lingering portion that survived?

If the answer to all three is yes, "residual" is your word.

Think of "residual" as the shadow of something that is mostly gone. The main substance, event, or feeling has passed through — resolved, consumed, removed, or treated — but it left a shadow behind. That shadow, still faintly present, still real, still measurable — is residual.
13737:
Residue is whatever is left behind after most of something has been removed, used up, consumed, or processed.

Think of it this way — something happens to a substance or a whole, and when the main action is over, there's a leftover portion that wasn't fully dealt with. That leftover is the residue.

Residue always implies a before and after. Something existed in a fuller or original form. Then a process happened — burning, washing, evaporating, filtering, reacting, spending, time passing. What survives that process, often in a smaller or altered form, is the residue. It is fundamentally the remainder — what was not consumed, not removed, not transformed away.

It is almost always smaller in quantity than the original thing. You don't usually call the bigger portion the residue; you call the leftover the residue.

When you wash a greasy pan but don't scrub thoroughly, there's a thin film of grease still clinging to the surface. That's residue. When you drink a glass of juice and there's a sticky coating left inside the glass, that's residue. When pesticides are sprayed on crops and traces remain on the fruit you buy at the store, those traces are called pesticide residue. When you peel a sticker off a surface and there's that annoying sticky patch left behind, that's adhesive residue.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: a substance was there, something happened (washing, drinking, peeling), but a portion stubbornly remained. That remainder is the residue.

This is where the word is used most precisely and technically. In chemistry, residue refers to the solid or concentrated material that remains after a substance has undergone a process such as evaporation, combustion (burning), filtration, or a chemical reaction.

For example: if you boil saltwater until all the water evaporates, you are left with solid salt crystals. Those crystals are the residue. If you burn wood completely, the ash left behind is the residue of the combustion process. If you filter a liquid through a fine mesh, the solid particles that the filter catches and holds back — unable to pass through — are called the residue (or filter residue).

In biochemistry and molecular biology, the word takes on a specific technical meaning: a residue is a single unit within a larger chain-like molecule. For example, proteins are long chains made of amino acids. Once an amino acid is bonded into that chain, it loses a small part of itself (a water molecule) in the bonding process. The portion of the amino acid that remains within the chain is called an amino acid residue. Similarly, in DNA, each nucleotide unit within the chain is called a nucleotide residue. Here, the word captures the idea of what remains of a unit after it has been incorporated into something larger.

In legal contexts, particularly in wills and inheritance, residue refers to what remains of a deceased person's estate after everything specific has been accounted for. When someone writes a will, they may leave specific items or amounts to specific people — "I leave my car to my son, $10,000 to my daughter, my gold watch to my nephew." After all those specific gifts are given out, and after all debts, taxes, and legal costs are paid, whatever is still left in the estate is called the residue of the estate. A will often includes a "residuary clause" that says who gets this residue. The person named to receive it is called the residuary beneficiary.

In mathematics, particularly in modular arithmetic (the math of remainders), the residue of a number is the remainder you get after dividing that number by another. For example, when you divide 17 by 5, you get 3 with a remainder of 2. That remainder, 2, is the residue of 17 with respect to 5. In more advanced mathematics (complex analysis), the term "residue" has a highly specific technical meaning related to the behavior of complex functions near certain special points, but that is a graduate-level concept.

Residue is also used in a non-physical, abstract sense to describe something intangible that lingers after an experience, event, or period of time. For example: "She carried the residue of childhood trauma well into adulthood." Here, the "residue" is the lasting psychological effect — the emotional leftover — of a painful past. Or: "There was a residue of bitterness in their relationship even after they reconciled." In these cases, the word paints a picture of something that wasn't fully cleared away, something that still clings on after the main event has ended.

Is residue always bad or unwanted? Not necessarily, though in everyday use it often refers to something undesirable — a dirty film, a chemical trace, an unpleasant lingering feeling. In scientific contexts, residue is simply a neutral, descriptive term with no judgment attached. The ash residue from a volcano can enrich soil and make it fertile. A residue in chemistry is simply what remains, neither good nor bad by definition.

Is residue always tiny? In general usage, yes — it implies a relatively small, often minor leftover. But in legal use, the residue of a wealthy estate could be enormous. The word doesn't technically demand smallness; it demands the quality of being what's left after other things have been taken away.

Residue vs. remnant vs. remainder: These words overlap but have different flavors. A remainder is the most neutral — simply what's left. A remnant often suggests a surviving fragment of something that was once larger or complete (like a remnant of an ancient civilization). Residue specifically emphasizes that something — a process, a reaction, an action — happened, and this is what that process left behind. The cause of the leftover is implied in the word residue.

Residue is the leftover — the portion that remains after a process has acted on something. Whether it's the soap film on a dish, the ash after burning, the chemical trace on food, the surviving fraction of a molecule in a biological chain, the remainder of an estate in a will, or the emotional echo of a past experience, the word always points to the same fundamental idea: something was here, something happened, and this is what did not go away.
13738: "Resign" has two separate meanings. Both are important, and knowing only one would give you an incomplete picture of the word.
Meaning 1: To voluntarily leave a job or official position

This is the most common use. When someone resigns, they choose to leave a job, a role, or an official position. They make that decision themselves — nobody forces them out.

Examples:

  • "The minister resigned after the scandal."
  • "She resigned from the board of directors."
  • "He resigned as captain of the team."

The act is usually formal. Resigning from a job typically involves writing a resignation letter and giving advance notice (telling your employer before your last day, not just walking out).

How "resign" differs from similar words — this is where learners often get confused

Resign vs. Quit
Both mean leaving voluntarily. The difference is tone and context. Resign is formal — it's used for professional jobs, political offices, and official roles. Quit is casual and can apply to almost anything ("I quit smoking," "I quit my part-time job"). A president resigns. A waiter might quit. Even if both words technically apply to a situation, "resign" signals seriousness and formality.

Resign vs. Retire
When you retire, you leave your career because you have completed it — usually after many years, often related to age. When you resign, you leave for your own personal reasons and at any point in your career. A 35-year-old cannot retire from a career, but can absolutely resign from a job.

Resign vs. Being Fired/Dismissed
This is the most important distinction. If you are fired, someone in authority removes you from your position — you had no choice. If you resign, you made the choice yourself. However, there is a grey area in real life: sometimes a person is put under intense pressure by others to leave, so they technically "choose" to resign, but the pressure was so great that it didn't feel like a real choice. This is called a forced resignation — and it sits somewhere between the two.

Grammar patterns for Meaning 1

The word is typically used in three ways:

  • Resign from (a place or organization) → She resigned from the company.
  • Resign as (a title or role) → He resigned as director.
  • Resign over (a reason) → She resigned over the controversy.

A special use in games

In chess and many other competitive games, to resign means to concede defeat before the game is officially over. A player sees that they are going to lose and, rather than play on pointlessly, they resign — meaning they formally accept defeat early. This is the same core idea: giving up a position, role, or standing voluntarily.
Meaning 2: To resign yourself to something

This is a completely different use of the word, with a completely different emotional meaning. When you resign yourself to something, you accept an unpleasant situation because you have realized you cannot change it. You stop fighting against it. You give in — not because you are happy, but because you see that there is no point in resisting any longer.

The emotion here is a mixture of acceptance, quiet defeat, and sometimes sadness. It is not the joyful acceptance of someone who got what they wanted. It is the heavy, reluctant acceptance of someone who has given up hope that things will be different.

Examples:

  • "After months of trying, she resigned herself to the fact that the project had failed."
  • "He resigned himself to waiting for hours with no complaint."
  • "The players resigned themselves to losing the match."

Grammar pattern for Meaning 2

This form always follows a fixed structure:

resign + oneself + to + (noun or verb ending in -ing)

  • I resigned myself to the delay.
  • She resigned herself to starting over.
  • They resigned themselves to never getting an answer.

The word oneself changes depending on who the subject is: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves. You cannot say "she resigned to the situation" — you must say "she resigned herself to the situation."

Both meanings of "resign" share a quiet underlying idea: giving something up willingly, even if painfully. In Meaning 1, you give up a position or role. In Meaning 2, you give up your resistance to a situation. The word is never about force from the outside — it is always about a personal decision, even when that decision is made under pressure or out of helplessness. That sense of personal, voluntary surrender — whether of a job or of hope — is the heart of the word.
13739: Resignation has two distinct meanings. Both share a hidden thread — the idea of giving something up or letting go — but they apply to very different situations. You need to know both.
Meaning 1: Voluntarily leaving a job or position

When a person chooses to leave their job, quit a role, or give up a position they hold, that act is called a resignation.

The critical word is voluntarily. A resignation is always the person's own decision. If someone is fired or removed by others, that is not a resignation. Resignation = you leaving on your own terms.

It applies broadly — leaving a job at a company, a politician stepping down from office, a member quitting a committee, an official withdrawing from a government role.

A resignation is usually formal. It's often put in writing as a resignation letter (also called a "letter of resignation") — a document that officially announces the person is leaving.

Examples:

  • "The CEO's resignation shocked the entire company." — The CEO chose to leave the role.
  • "She wrote her resignation and placed it on her manager's desk." — Here "resignation" refers to the letter itself.
  • "The minister's resignation came after weeks of scandal."

Common verb pairings:

  • Submit / hand in / tender a resignation → to formally give the letter to the relevant person
  • Accept a resignation → to officially acknowledge that someone is leaving
Meaning 2: Quiet, calm acceptance of something unpleasant

This is the more emotional, abstract meaning — and it's equally common, especially in literature and thoughtful writing.

When you face a difficult, painful, or unwanted situation that you cannot change, and you stop fighting it, stop resisting, and simply accept it — even if that acceptance feels sad or reluctant — that state of mind is called resignation.

Picture it this way: resignation is the feeling behind the thought, "I don't like this. I wish things were different. But they aren't, and there's nothing I can do — so I'll accept it and move on."

This is not cheerful, happy acceptance. It carries a quiet, slightly heavy, even defeated tone. You are not at peace with the situation; you have simply stopped fighting it. It is acceptance without joy.

Examples:

  • "He faced his illness with resignation, knowing the doctors could do nothing more." — He accepted his illness calmly, without bitterness, because fighting it was no longer possible.
  • "She signed the divorce papers with a sigh of resignation." — She accepted something painful that she could not undo.
  • "There was resignation in her voice as she said goodbye." — Her tone was that quiet, subdued sound of someone who has accepted something they cannot change.
  • "He shrugged with resignation and went back to work." — He accepted an annoying or unfair situation without making a fuss, because he knew it wouldn't change.

Common phrases with this meaning:

  • With resignation — in a tone or manner of quiet acceptance
  • A sense of resignation / a feeling of resignation — that emotional state of having stopped resisting
  • Resigned to something (the adjective form, related to this meaning) — having accepted something, e.g., "She was resigned to the fact that she wouldn't get the job."
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context makes it almost always obvious:

  • If the sentence involves a job, office, role, or position and someone is leaving it → Meaning 1
    • "His resignation from the board was unexpected."
  • If the sentence describes a feeling, attitude, reaction, or tone in the face of something difficult → Meaning 2
    • "She accepted the bad news with resignation."

Both meanings share a common core: letting go of something. In Meaning 1, you let go of a position or role. In Meaning 2, you let go of the struggle against something you cannot control. This is not a coincidence — it is what gives the word its depth. Whether you are leaving a job or accepting a painful reality, you are, in both cases, releasing your hold on something.

That is what resignation means — and now you know all of it.
